1. Baseline: For values v<30 bid 0; 30–60 bid floor(0.4v); 61–80 bid floor(0.6v); >80 bid floor(0.75v).  
2. Aggressive test: Occasionally (e.g., 20% of rounds) bid v or v–1 when v≥60 to probe rivals’ ceiling.  
3. Shading experiment: For mid values (40–70), alternate between 0.5v and 0.7v to estimate win probabilities.  
4. Adaptive updates: After each round, adjust target markup (v–bid) by +/–5 based on observed rivals’ max bids, aiming to win when v – expected rival max > expected loss from overbidding.

1. Early exploration (Rounds 1–3):  
   - Map others’ aggressiveness.  
   - Use value-dependent randomization:  
     • v<30: bid 0–10 uniformly.  
     • 30≤v<70: bid around 40–80% of v with noise ±5.  
     • v≥70: sometimes overbid up to v+15 to test thresholds.  

2. Model-building (Rounds 4–6):  
   - Infer opponents’ bid distributions conditional on value ranges from observed behavior.  
   - Test slightly under/over aggressive variants near inferred winning thresholds.  

3. Exploitation (Rounds 7–10):  
   - Bid just above estimated winning threshold; reduce bids sharply when win probability is low.

1. Start with mildly aggressive shading: bid ≈ 0.7·value for v≤60, 0.8·value for v>60, to gauge others’ aggressiveness.  
2. Track, per value range, win frequency, average rival bids, and profit.  
3. If rivals underbid (win margins >10 on average), test more aggressive rules: 0.8–0.9·value, especially for v>50.  
4. If rivals overbid (frequent negative profits when winning), test conservative rules: 0.4–0.6·value.  
5. Occasionally (e.g., 10–20% of rounds) randomize within ±10 of planned bid to explore and avoid predictability.
